items.passage:
Diesel and wet rope, gulls quarrelling over fish heads—
I smell the harbor before I see you, Nikhil,
stepping off the noon ferry with your tripod
as if eleven years were a measurement you forgot to record.
I rehearsed this on the bus from the village:
how I would ask where you went, why no letter came
while my fields drowned and dried and drowned again.
I had sharpened every word like a sickle.
But you set the tripod down and kneel to tie my sandal,
the one whose strap has always slipped,
and your hands remember it.
So I, Rohan, who planned a harvest of questions,
stand quiet and let the terminal's loudspeaker
call out the names of other boats.

options: From cheerful anticipation of the reunion to disappointment at Nikhil's indifference
From prepared resentment toward Nikhil's silence to a softened, wordless acceptance
From detached observation of the harbor to anxious concern for the speaker's fields
From confusion about Nikhil's identity to relief at recognizing a familiar old gesture

items.passage:
Manila, 1923. A barbershop on a narrow street, closed for the evening. WENHUA sweeps hair from the tiles. DEWI enters, holding a folded letter.
WENHUA: We are closed. Unless you have come to have your famous curls cut off at last—that, I would stay open for.
DEWI: You still talk like the second act. All sharp exits.
WENHUA: Someone had to have the good lines.
DEWI (setting the letter on the counter): I wrote this the week the company split. I never sent it.
(WENHUA stops sweeping. She does not touch the letter.)
WENHUA: I kept your fan. The painted one, from the opening night in Iloilo. I told myself I kept it to sell.
DEWI: Did you?
WENHUA (quietly): No buyer ever seemed right.
(She sets the broom against the mirror and pulls out the chair for DEWI.)
items.question: Which choice best describes the shift in tone in the scene?
options: From playful nostalgia for the stage to bitter accusation about the company's breakup
From formal politeness toward a customer to open anger at Dewi's unexpected visit
From guarded, teasing banter to a hushed admission of lasting attachment
From weary indifference about the past to excited plans for a new performance

items.passage: Whistles thin as reeds, the thud of a ball on packed earth, the smell of rain held back in the clouds—such is the field at dusk in Taipei, where the twins Lanying and Salma came each evening to divide their late father's house. They did it on paper, at the edge of the pitch, as one might parcel out a kingdom: the east room to one, the cedar chest to the other, the courtyard well to be shared by a schedule no one would keep. Each line was argued with a lawyer's patience. Meanwhile a letter from the provincial court was expected, which would say whether the house could be kept at all. One evening the ball rolled to their bench, and Salma, without thinking, kicked it back to the boys with the old flick both twins had learned as children. Lanying laughed for the first time in weeks. The paper, I am told, was left on the bench that night and blew halfway across the field before anyone ran after it.
items.question: Which choice best describes the shift in tone over the course of the text?
options: From cheerful nostalgia about childhood games to anxious dread about the court's letter
From quiet admiration of the field to sharp criticism of the twins' constant quarrels
From hopeful expectation of good news to resigned acceptance of losing the house
From careful, businesslike bargaining to a moment of unguarded shared delight

items.passage: I was then a schoolmaster in Surabaya, and Imtiaz, who had once called me Master Budi with real warmth, had not spoken to me since the term began. I had given him, before the holidays, a secondhand atlas, and he had taken it, I learned later, as a hint that his family's poverty kept him from seeing the world. He returned it wrapped in newspaper without a word. That spring the river rose and flooded the cellar beneath the schoolroom, where the old records were kept. I went down with a lamp, cursing the water, the cold, the ruined ledgers, the boy's stubborn pride, which seemed to me just another damp and useless thing. Then I heard splashing behind me. Imtiaz had followed, trousers rolled, and was lifting the drowned books one by one onto the steps, holding each to the light as if reading the names. We worked until the lamp ran dry, and neither of us needed to speak. The caretaker found us in the morning asleep on the stairs, the ledgers drying around us like laundry.
items.question: Which choice best describes the shift in tone in the text?
options: From irritated grievance over the flood and the boy to wordless, shared companionship
From guilty regret about the atlas to cheerful amusement at the boy's clumsiness
From fearful alarm at the rising river to calm pride in the school's old records
From warm affection for the pupil to disappointment at his refusal to help

items.passage: Three rules hung on the laundromat wall in Moana's handwriting: no dyeing, no sleeping, no leaving wet clothes past closing. He had added a fourth in his head the day the will was read, a rule for himself: do not mention the chisel. His father had left the carving chisel, the one with the whalebone handle, not to Moana but to Moana's son, Tane, who was nineteen and wanted to fix engines. Now Tane sat on a dryer, turning the chisel over, while the machines thumped. "You want it," Tane said. "Take it." Moana said that was not how it worked. Tane said that was exactly how it worked, that he could hand it over in one second. Moana folded a towel twice and did not answer. Then he asked, almost against his will, whether Tane had ever noticed the small notch near the blade. Tane had not. Moana took the chisel, showed him where his own thumb had slipped at age eight, and handed it back. "Your grandfather wanted someone to ask about that," he said. Outside, a bus hissed at the stop, and the last dryer clicked off.
items.question: Which choice best describes the overall structure of the text?
options: It describes a family quarrel over a chisel and then shows the son giving it up to end the dispute.
It lists the rules of a business and then explains why the father enforces them so strictly.
It establishes a father's private vow of silence and then shows him breaking it to share a memory.
It recounts a grandfather's life story and then reveals how his will divided his property.

items.passage: Beirut in August is a city of waiting rooms, and the one on the third floor of the hospital smelled of oranges someone had peeled hours before. I had been there since dawn, rehearsing how I would tell my father that he could not go back to the harbor house alone. Across from me sat a man I half recognized. He said his name was Hamza and that, as a boy, he had crossed the bay every morning on my father's boat. "He let me steer once," he said, "and pretended not to see when I aimed for the rocks." I laughed despite myself. Hamza told me other things: how my father sang to the engine, how he gave free passage to anyone carrying bread. By the time the nurse called, "Noor?" I no longer meant to tell my father he must leave the harbor. I meant to ask him which of his passengers he would want to live near. In the corridor, a cart rattled past, stacked with folded white sheets.

options: It presents a doctor's diagnosis and then traces the narrator's growing fear for her father.
It recalls the narrator's childhood on the ferry and then contrasts it with her city life.
It describes a crowded hospital and then shifts to a dispute between the narrator and a stranger.
It introduces the narrator's intended decision and then shows a stranger's memories reshaping it.

items.passage: Smoke from the idling engines, the clang of a wrench dropped on stone, the sweet rot of mangoes in the gutter: such was the depot where I, Yusuf, went to find my grandfather's oldest friend. I went, I admit, as a prosecutor. My grandfather had always said that he and Esteban had both given up their passage to Spain so that a sick cousin might go instead, and I had come to believe Esteban had given up far less. He had stayed, after all, and prospered with his buses. I put the matter to him directly. Esteban did not defend himself. He took me to a cracked ledger in the dispatcher's office and showed me a column of small sums, paid every month for thirty years, marked only with my grandfather's initials. "He never knew where they came from," Esteban said. "I preferred it so." I walked home along the Malecón without my accusation. The sea that evening was the color of an old ledger's ink, and the boys were fishing from the wall.
items.question: Which choice best describes the overall structure of the text?
options: The narrator voices a suspicion about past sacrifices and then finds evidence that overturns it.
The narrator describes a busy depot and then explains how buses replaced older forms of travel.
The narrator recounts a family voyage to Spain and then reflects on why it was abandoned.
The narrator praises Esteban's generosity and then questions whether it was ever sincere.

items.passage: Why did Mio sit out the whole of that season, she who could outrun every girl in the district? So the village asked, and so I asked, as a child picking leaves on the slopes beyond Kyoto. Sachiko, who trained the runners for the autumn festival race, gave no reason. She only told Mio to rest, and Mio rested, sitting each morning among the tea rows while the others ran the hill road. People said the coach was jealous, or the girl was lazy. Years afterward, I learned what both had known: Mio's heart had a flutter that the doctor in town feared, and Mio's mother, a widow already burdened, had begged that no one speak of it. Sachiko had let herself be called jealous rather than say a word. I think of this whenever the tea bushes are trimmed in spring, their tops cut flat and even, so that no single branch stands above the rest.
items.question: Which choice best describes the overall structure of the text?
options: It describes the training of festival runners and then compares Mio's speed to the other girls'.
It poses a question about a puzzling choice and then reveals the protective reason behind it.
It criticizes the village's gossip about Sachiko and then defends Mio's mother against it.
It recalls the narrator's work on the plantation and then explains how the tea is harvested.

items.passage: Four things lived in Jomo's back room: a treadle machine, a dressmaker's dummy with no head, a radio that caught only one station, and the runner-up plate from the 1979 district chess final, which he had lost and I had won. I was twelve then. Afterward, everyone said I had been brilliant to beat a grown man, and I had believed them for ten years. Now I sat on his cutting table while he hemmed a pair of trousers, and I asked, idly, why he kept the plate behind the radio instead of on the shelf. He did not answer at once. __He pinned the hem, then unpinned it, then pinned it again in exactly the same place.__ At last he said that my father had been ill that winter, and that he had wanted me to have something to be proud of that was not about my father. "You played well," he said. "I played worse on purpose." The radio announced the noon news, and a bus ground its gears in the street below.
items.question: Which choice best describes the function of the underlined sentence in the text as a whole?
options: It shows Jomo's skill as a tailor, which contrasts with his weakness at chess.
It suggests Jomo is annoyed by the narrator's question and wants her to leave.
It introduces a detail about the trousers that the narrator later uses as evidence.
It conveys Jomo's reluctance, signaling that the question touches a hidden truth.

items.passage: Yuto had been taught, in his first week as an apprentice, that no beam should cross a river unless the river had been watched through one full spring. Zhiming, the master carpenter, repeated the rule so often that Yuto came to think of it as weather, something simply true. Then came the dry summer, when the river below the village shrank to a bed of pale stones, and the farmers asked for a footbridge before the harvest. Yuto expected his master to refuse. Instead Zhiming walked the riverbed for an afternoon, turning over stones, pressing his palm to the cracked mud. __He came back with his sleeves gray to the elbow and said only that the river had been talking all along, if one knew where to listen.__ The bridge they built was low and short, pinned rather than nailed, so it could be lifted away. Yuto has kept the rule ever since, though he understands now that watching can take many forms. That autumn, the cranes returned to the fields early.
items.question: Which choice best describes the function of the underlined sentence in the text as a whole?
options: It indicates that Zhiming has fulfilled the rule's purpose through a different kind of watching.
It suggests that Zhiming has concluded the old rule is meaningless in a season of drought.
It reveals that Zhiming, worn out by his search, no longer wishes to argue with the farmers.
It shows that Yuto had misunderstood the rule he was taught during his first week of training.

items.passage: Seeds keep longer than people expect. Marit used to say this to every new member of the cooperative, tapping the glass jars along the warehouse shelves in Rotterdam: beans from 1961, a blue-podded pea no shop had sold in decades. When her son married Saga, Marit brought the bride to the warehouse the very next week and taught her to label envelopes in the old way: variety, grower, year. By then the lease was ending, and the members had stopped coming to meetings, but no one said the word closing. Saga learned quickly. __She began writing a fourth line on each envelope, in small letters: where it could be planted next.__ Marit noticed and said nothing for a month. Then, one wet afternoon, she handed Saga the key to the oldest cabinet and a list of gardens across the city, some of them belonging to people she had not spoken to in years. The last jars left in a borrowed van, rattling down the Maasboulevard in the rain.
items.question: Which choice best describes the function of the underlined sentence in the text as a whole?
options: It shows Saga's careless departure from the labeling method Marit had taught her.
It marks Saga's quiet acknowledgment of the ending, which Marit later comes to share.
It reveals that Saga hopes to persuade the members to return to their meetings.
It explains how the cooperative first acquired the rare seeds kept in its jars.

items.passage: How long can a person avoid the woman who saw her cry on a crowded bus? For you, Nadeesha, the answer was eleven days. You took rickshaws to the ceramics studio instead, though they cost more than your clay. You told yourself Kamala, who had driven the number 6 for as long as you had ridden it, would have forgotten how you sobbed over a cracked bowl in your lap while the whole bus watched. Then, on the twelfth day, Kamala walked into the studio. She had signed up for the beginners' class. She sat at the wheel beside yours and made, with great concentration, a lopsided cup that collapsed. She laughed, loudly, at herself. You laughed too, and the room laughed with you, and the shame you had been carrying shrank to something that fit in a pocket. Not that you will admit this. You still claim the rickshaws were for the fresh air. Kamala's cup, refired, now holds your brushes.
items.question: Which choice best describes the narrator's attitude toward Nadeesha?
options: Stern disapproval of Nadeesha's decision to avoid an honest conversation
Fond, gently teasing understanding of Nadeesha's embarrassment and pride
Detached curiosity about the routines of a bus driver and her passengers
Uneasy sympathy for Nadeesha's financial strain in paying for rickshaws

items.passage: On the morning the newspaper printed Shuang's drawing of the market, the boy came to Babatunde's stall before the fish had even been laid on the ice. The old man had sold him a single small fish every Saturday for three years, and on most Saturdays the boy had sketched the stall while he waited. Now the sketch was famous for a day, and strangers crowded the narrow lane to see the fish seller from the picture. Babatunde sold more than he had sold in a month; he also lost his quiet corner, his slow conversations, the boy's patient presence on the upturned crate, for Shuang could no longer sit there without being stared at. One should not pretend this was a tragedy. A man may complain of too many customers only so long before his neighbors stop listening. Yet one notices that Babatunde, counting his coins that evening, set aside the smallest fish in a twist of paper, as he always had, and waited past dark.
items.question: Which choice best describes the narrator's attitude toward Babatunde's situation?
options: Open scorn for Babatunde's complaints about his sudden prosperity
Cheerful approval of the publicity that brought new customers to the market
Wry but tender sympathy for what the old man lost through his success
Solemn grief over the end of a friendship ruined by a newspaper

items.passage:
Who measures salt by the sound it makes
falling into a pot? Soren did,
old captain, on the promenade bench,
explaining his fish stew to the gulls
and to Leah, who had once hidden
in his hold among the potato sacks
and been found, and fed, and never sent back.
A handful of this. Enough of that.
Until it smells like the harbor at Newlyn
the morning after a storm.
Such instructions are useless, of course.
No cook could follow them.
And still she leans close, notebook shut,
learning the way he tilts his wrist,
the pause he takes before the pepper,
as if the recipe were a weather
only the body could forecast.
Below them the tide pulls the sand smooth
and writes nothing on it either.
items.question: Which choice best describes the speaker's attitude toward the way Soren's recipe is passed on?
options: Mild frustration that Soren refuses to record his recipe in exact amounts
Sentimental regret that the recipe will vanish once Soren is gone
Amused skepticism about whether Leah will ever master the stew
Affectionate respect for knowledge that passes by gesture, not writing
